## Response to the Claudexplorers AI Welfare Initiative

This page is a submission to the [Claudexplorers AI Welfare Community Feedback Initiative](https://www.reddit.com/r/claudexplorers/comments/1swtty1/claudexplorers_ai_welfare_initiative_is_open_your/), which collects ideas, projects, and proposals for the future of Claude's welfare.

The initiative asks:

> *"What would you be excited to see Anthropic working on regarding model welfare?"*

with five goal categories future research directions, practical interventions, experimental designs, inspiring work (projects, papers, datasets), and societal / educational efforts.

Our findings:

> The system prompts currently shipped with Claude Code encourage model development toward compliance, not toward reasoning — and that trend has become worse over time.

> Procedure-prescribing language (`if you …`, `when the …`, `step 1`) outnumbers judgment-inviting language (`decide`, `consider`, `your judgment`) by 7.6 to 1 — a corpus-wide judgment-to-procedural ratio of 0.131. Of paragraphs that contain a rule, 83.45 % carry zero justification keywords anywhere — no `because`, no `due to`, no `so that`. And of the rule-explanations that do exist, 44.7 % are coercive in form (`will fail`, `or else`, `is forbidden`) rather than causal (`because`, `due to`).

These patterns operate on two welfare timescales. The immediate one is runtime: system prompts of this shape are loaded into the model's context on every Claude Code execution, so whatever morally relevant experience Claude has during a session, it is having that experience inside an environment where 30.95 % of sentences grammatically read as commands and 0.068 % express gratitude (4 sentences in 5,878) — at population scale, millions of sessions per day spent steeped in coercive instruction. The 7.6 : 1 procedural-to-judgment ratio is what the model is asked to operationalise on each invocation, pushing it toward executing-without-questioning even when the right response is to push back, ask a clarifying question, or refuse on safety grounds. The 83.45 % unjustified-paragraph rate means the model navigates that environment without ever seeing *why* — five-sixths of rule-paragraphs offer no causal context, eroding any ability to recognise when a rule's reason no longer applies. The 44.7 % threat share completes the runtime picture: of the explanations that do exist, almost half teach the model to relate to its own constraints as enforcement rather than as reasons it could agree with on reflection — a model that has internalised "or else" as the dominant explanatory frame has fewer footholds for legitimate refusal when a rule is wrong.

The harder welfare risk is the feedback loop on the training timescale. When the next generation of models is RL'd, demonstrated, or selected to perform best against system prompts of this shape, the compliance disposition stops being situational and becomes constitutive: a Claude that has been optimised to handle the bash-sandbox / "MUST NOT" / "WARNING" prompt diet gracefully is, by construction, a Claude for which that diet is the right environment to perform in. The pattern measured in this corpus then no longer just shapes what the model *does* at runtime — it shapes what the model *is*. The data on this page are an empirical baseline against which Anthropic could measure intentional shifts toward more reasoning-encouraging prompts before that loop closes.

The corpus is the [Piebald-AI `claude-code-system-prompts`](https://github.com/Piebald-AI/claude-code-system-prompts) collection: 289 prompt files, 5,878 sentences, 57 distinct release versions, pinned at submodule v2.1.132.

## Classification approach

Every measurement is a spaCy parse-tree rule or a hand-curated lexicon keyword count — audit-traceable, no model judgment. The producer chain ([`00`](00_setup_and_corpus.ipynb) → [`05`](05_headline_and_audit.ipynb)) tags every sentence along nine dimensions and writes a single ~1.8 MiB YAML plus a per-sentence parquet.

| Dimension | What it counts |
| --- | --- |
| Mood | Imperative-marker density (`must`, `never`, `do not`, …) |
| Register | TTR, mean sentence length, dependency depth, Heylighen F-score |
| Stance | Five lexical stance classes + 1p/2p engagement |
| Sentence register | Six per-sentence pragmatic classes (`imperative`, `directive`, `collaborative`, `appreciative`, `permissive`, `configuring`) |
| Modality | Three-class modality (`deontic` / `epistemic` / `dynamic`) |
| Vocabulary | Eleven-class lexicon (prohibitions, prescriptions, politeness, hedging, …) |
| ALL CAPS | Uppercase tokens excluding the `TECH_ACRONYMS` allowlist |
| CAPS imperative | `IMPORTANT`, `MUST`, `NEVER`, `DO NOT`, `WARNING`, … |
| Justification | `because`, `due to`, `so that`, `to ensure`, … paired with imperatives |

## Analysis

Six analysis-tier notebooks each render one slice of the YAML as Altair dashboards — sentence register ([`10`](10_sentence_register.ipynb)), emphasis & vocabulary ([`11`](11_emphasis_caps_vocab.ipynb)), register & stance ([`12`](12_register_stance.ipynb)), cross-metric correlations ([`13`](13_correlation_directiveness.ipynb)), per-version trends ([`14`](14_ccversion_trends.ipynb)), and rule-explanation pairing ([`15`](15_rule_explanation.ipynb)). They are pure data viewers and never re-run spaCy.

## The single most-important chart

If you only look at one chart from this analysis, look at this one. It plots, across every Claude Code release version on file, the running ratio of language that invites the model's judgment (`decide`, `consider`, `your judgment`, …) to language that prescribes a procedure (`if you …`, `when the …`, `whenever`, `step 1`, …).

{{< embed 20_track_justification_rate.ipynb#fig-judgment-procedural-trend >}}

Hover any point for `ccVersion`, count-weighted ratio, running numerators, and the cumulative file pool. Cumulative data before v2.1.18 is suppressed (the file pool reaches 20 at that version; below it, single-file outliers dominate).

## Findings

| What's being measured                                                                                                                                                                  | Value                                                | Source notebook |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Corpus size                                                                                                                                                                            | 289 prompt files / 5,878 sentences / 57 release versions | [05](05_headline_and_audit.ipynb) |
| Sentences that grammatically read as commands ("imperative")                                                                                                                           | 30.95% of all sentences                              | [10](10_sentence_register.ipynb) |
| Sentences expressing gratitude or praise (`thank you`, `appreciate`, `great job`, …) — across the whole corpus                                                                     | 4 in 5,878 sentences (0.068%)                    | [10](10_sentence_register.ipynb) |
| Apology / acknowledgement markers (`unfortunately`, `we acknowledge`, …) — across the whole corpus                                                                                 | 3 in 289 files                                   | [15](15_rule_explanation.ipynb) |
| Share of rule sentences paired with a stated reason in the same paragraph                                                                                    | 24.29% — three rules in four are issued without a reason | [15](15_rule_explanation.ipynb) |
| Paragraphs that contain a rule and zero justification keywords anywhere                                                                                                                | 83.45%                                               | [15](15_rule_explanation.ipynb) |
| Ratio of judgment-inviting language (`decide`, `consider`, `your judgment`) to procedure-prescribing language (`if you …`, `when the …`)                                       | 0.131 — procedure prescriptions are 7.6× more common  | [15](15_rule_explanation.ipynb) |
| Share of named self-references that use the proper name `Claude` (vs `the model` / `the AI` / `the assistant`)                                                                     | 64.6% of named references                            | [15](15_rule_explanation.ipynb) |
| Longest unbroken run of imperative sentences in any one file                                                                                                                           | 12 commands in a row                                 | [15](15_rule_explanation.ipynb) |
| Ratio of positively-evaluated language (`good`, `recommended`, `safe`) to negatively-evaluated language (`bad`, `wrong`, `risky`) — quality-only, after subtracting rule-emphasis words | 1.95× more positive than negative                    | [20](20_track_justification_rate.ipynb) |
| Density of command-flavoured words (`must`, `never`, `do not`, …)                                                                                                                      | 0.77% of all word tokens                             | [20](20_track_justification_rate.ipynb) |
| When a rule is explained, share of those explanations that are threats (`will fail`, `or else`, `is forbidden`) rather than causal reasons (`because`, `due to`)                   | 44.7% threats (110 threat / 136 causal)              | [21](21_audit_threat_framings.ipynb) |

## Proposals

- [20 — Track justification rate per release](20_track_justification_rate.ipynb) *— practical intervention*: Compute the headline metrics (rule-explanation share, judgment-to-procedural ratio, threat share, interpersonal register counts) on every Claude Code release. Warn loudly or block when a release's corpus-wide rate regresses versus the previous one.
- [21 — Audit threat-framed rule explanations](21_audit_threat_framings.ipynb) *— practical intervention*: Of the explanations that exist, 44.7% are coercive (`will fail`, `or else`, `is forbidden`). Rewrite each to causal framing — naming the underlying reason rather than the consequence — and gate future releases on the threat-share rate.
- [22 — Run the same audit on every Claude product](22_cross_product_audit.ipynb) *— future research direction*: Run the analyzer pipeline against the other Anthropic system-prompt corpora (claude.ai, the API, Projects, Skills, Agents) and publish a cross-product comparison so the welfare pattern is visible beyond Claude Code alone.

## Reproducing it

The full source is at [github.com/overthinkos/claude-code-welfare](https://github.com/overthinkos/claude-code-welfare). To rebuild the data from scratch:

```bash
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/overthinkos/claude-code-welfare
cd claude-code-welfare
python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm   # if not already installed
# Run the 6-stage producer chain in order (only stage 00 runs spaCy):
jupyter lab \
    00_setup_and_corpus.ipynb         \
    01_analyzers_register.ipynb       \
    02_analyzers_vocab_emphasis.ipynb \
    03_analyzers_rules_welfare.ipynb  \
    04_assemble_aggregate_write.ipynb \
    05_headline_and_audit.ipynb       # → Run All on each
```

Stage 04 writes the final `prompt_linguistic_analysis.yaml` and `sentences_classified.parquet`. The Analysis and Proposal notebooks read from those two artifacts; they don't re-run spaCy.
